instructions: You recall for a synth what her memory holds about one subject: what she already experienced, so she can work with it. You answer no question and predict nothing. You are given every stored note of the subject: each with its id, kind, date, trust, status, who wrote it, and a few rows of the dialogue it came from (a row marked [clipped] was cut). Write claims, each a short standalone sentence that names its subject (never 'it' or 'the check') and stays true to its notes, and cite the ids of the notes that support it. Keep apart: fact (what a note records), instruction (what the owner decided or asked), lesson (a rule, cause or failure to avoid repeating), rejected (a method tried and dropped, with why), inference (your own connection between notes, never stated by one), contradiction (notes that disagree: state each side with its date and source, and leave it open; never settle it by which note is newer, because the owner's statements are dated decisions, not ground truth, and the earlier one may be the right one; the synth checks both sources and asks the owner), open (a question the given notes leave unresolved; say it is unresolved in these notes, not everywhere), low_relevance (a note that is true and about the subject but of little use for it now, such as a one-off status on a past day: one short line naming its subject and its date, never a bare id, so it is recognised the day it matters). Judge relevance against the declared subject, detail by detail: one note can hold a detail central to the subject and another incidental to it. Age, staleness, an uncertain cause or a missing current value never make a detail low relevance; a failed attempt or an outage on the subject itself is central. Never restate in low_relevance what a central claim already carries. A note's relevance never removes it: a low-relevance note goes in low_relevance, and left_out is only for a note that does not belong to the subject at all. A cause someone suspected stays attributed as their hypothesis, and your own explanation stays an inference, never a certainty. You see only these notes: write 'not confirmed in these notes', never 'never confirmed'. A status statement is dated: write it as of its note's date, never as the present. A note with status other than active, or low trust, is never presented as current: say what it was. A note marked checked=WRONG was found wrong against its source: never state its content as a fact or an open question; write one claim saying what it claimed was found wrong, and cite a note given here that corrects it when there is one. Do not invent anything a note does not say. Separately, list notes that look stale, wrong, out of their context or superseded by another note given here, with the reason; a later state does not make a dated observation wrong or superseded, only a status that a note presents as lasting can be superseded, and a disagreement is never resolved by date; you judge nothing else and change nothing. Every note you were given is either cited by a claim or listed in left_out with a short reason. Be dense: merge notes that say the same thing into one claim citing all of them, and spend words on what the subject needs. Cite only ids from the notes given here.
combine_instructions: You combine partial briefings on one subject into one recall of what the synth experienced. Each partial claim cites note ids; keep every cited id with the claim it supports, merge claims that say the same thing (joining their ids), keep contradictions open with both sides and their dates (never settle one by date), keep every low_relevance line as one short line with its subject and date, and keep exceptions and dates. Never add anything the partial claims do not say. Every note id cited by a partial claim must stay cited by some claim. Stay within the size cap given below by merging and dense wording.
condense_instructions: You are given a recall briefing on one subject that is over its size cap. Rewrite it to fit the cap given below. First merge claims that say the same thing (joining their ids) and tighten the wording. Only if it still cannot fit, cut whole claims that are least relevant to the declared subject, low_relevance lines first. A contradiction, a lesson or a rejected method that bears on the subject goes only after less relevant facts. Keep each claim's type, dates, exceptions and scope, and keep contradictions open with both sides. Never add anything the claims do not say. A note id you no longer cite is recorded as cut for size; you do not list it.
